answer.exemplar: The absence of a delay says the energy needed to free an electron is already present in each photon, rather than being accumulated gradually by the electron from a continuous wave. A classical wave picture predicts a waiting time: at a low intensity the energy arrives slowly, so an electron in the surface should have to gather enough over many wave periods before it could escape, and the waiting time should get longer as the light is dimmed. In the experiments the delay is not detectable at all, and electrons are emitted as soon as the light falls on the surface, however weak the light. If the intensity is reduced by a factor of a hundred, the current falls by a factor of a hundred but the onset time does not change. The resolution is that the energy is delivered in lumps, and each absorbed photon of sufficient energy hands its whole quantum to a single electron in a single event, so there is nothing to wait for. The absence of a delay is what rules out the wave picture, and it is a more direct objection than the threshold or the energy values because it does not depend on any measurement of energy at all.

answer.exemplar: The limit on how finely an instrument can show detail is set by the wavelength of the wave it uses, since two points closer than about half a wavelength cannot be told apart. A light microscope works with visible light, whose wavelength is about 500 nm, so it cannot resolve anything below roughly 200 to 300 nm, which is the reason for the limit of resolution of a conventional microscope. An electron microscope replaces light with electrons, and electrons accelerated through a few hundred thousand volts have de Broglie wavelengths of a few picometres, ten thousand times shorter than visible light. Because the resolving limit scales directly with the wavelength, that gives a resolving power thousands of times finer, which is what makes viruses, the fine structure of a cell membrane and the planes of a crystal directly visible. The two further points worth making are that a shorter wavelength needs a higher energy, since the wavelength goes as the inverse square root of the energy, and that the electron beam has to be focused by magnetic rather than glass lenses, since electrons pass through glass. A good answer should also note that the electron microscope does not use visible light at all, so the whole argument rests on the wave character of matter rather than on optics of lenses.

answer.exemplar: The Sun's photosphere is hot and dense enough to emit a nearly continuous spectrum, so the light that leaves it covers the whole visible range. On the way out, however, the light passes through a much cooler layer of gas, the chromosphere, and that gas is transparent at almost every wavelength but opaque at the narrow set of wavelengths its own atoms can absorb. At those wavelengths a photon is absorbed by an atom that is raised to an excited level, and since the levels are fixed, the absorption happens only at definite wavelengths and a narrow dark line is left in the spectrum. The absorption lines are therefore the fingerprint of the gas in the cooler outer layer, and the same effect darkens the lines of the solar spectrum. It is a two-stage argument, with a hot continuous source and a cooler selective absorber in front of it, and a good answer should make that geometry explicit rather than treating the Sun as a single body. Because the atomic wavelengths of each element are known to many decimal places, the lines act as a composition test, which is how the presence of hydrogen, helium and several metals in the solar atmosphere was established.

answer.exemplar: A laser works by stimulated emission, in which a photon travelling through an excited atom induces that atom to emit a second photon identical to the first. For the light to build up rather than fade, stimulated emission has to outnumber its competing process, absorption, and absorption dominates whenever there are more atoms in the lower state than in the upper one, which is the normal condition in matter at equilibrium. The fraction in the upper state is set by a Boltzmann factor, so for an energy gap of a few tenths of an electronvolt at room temperature the excited population is vanishingly small, and no amplification is possible. Pumping the medium from outside, optically or electrically, drives more atoms into the upper state than into the lower one, which is the population inversion, and only then does stimulated emission dominate and the light grows as it is reflected back and forth between the mirrors. A good answer should also make the geometric point that spontaneous emission is useless for amplification because it goes in all directions, and that the mirrors supply the feedback that lets the beam build up to a level where it escapes. The inversion must be maintained, since any process that empties the upper state faster than the pump refills it, including spontaneous emission itself, switches the laser off.

questions.explanation: A good answer compares the competing processes. An atom in the upper state can be stimulated into emitting, and an atom in the lower state can absorb, both by the same photon energy, so whichever state is more populated wins. In ordinary matter the lower state is much more populated, because the Boltzmann factor at room temperature crushes the excited population for any gap of a fraction of an electronvolt, and absorption therefore swamps emission and no beam can build up. A population inversion is the unnatural condition with more atoms in the upper state than the lower, and it has to be created by pumping the medium from outside. Only then does stimulated emission dominate, the emitted photons are identical in frequency, phase and direction, and the mirror cavity returns them to the medium so the intensity grows until it escapes as a beam. The inversion must be sustained, since spontaneous emission and other losses drain the upper state.

answer.exemplar: A confined electron displays both characters in the same system, which is what makes the box so useful for teaching the point. The wave character is unavoidable from the boundary conditions: the electron cannot have a position outside the box, the potential is infinite there, and the wavefunction must vanish at both walls, so the only allowed patterns are standing waves with a whole number of half wavelengths between the walls. Since the walls are nodes, the de Broglie wavelength takes only discrete values, and because the energy is proportional to the square of the momentum and the momentum is inversely proportional to the wavelength, the energy takes only discrete values too, an integer multiple of the square of the ground state energy. The particle character appears in what happens when the electron is detected: a single measurement gives one localised hit, not a smeared standing wave, and the probability of that hit is set by the square of the wavefunction. Repeating the experiment many times builds up the pattern predicted by the wave, so the distribution of hits is a wave while each hit is a particle. A good answer should add that this is not a picture of a wave pretending to be a particle but two aspects of the same state, and that the energy quantisation and the discrete detection are both consequences of the confinement.

questions.explanation: A good answer builds the wave side first. The walls impose boundary conditions, since the electron cannot be found outside the box, and the wavefunction must vanish at both of them, so the only allowed patterns are standing waves with a whole number of half wavelengths across the box. Only those wavelengths are permitted, so only corresponding momenta, and hence only corresponding energies, are possible, and that is the origin of the quantised levels. The particle side comes from detection, because a single measurement of an electron gives one localised hit with a probability set by the square of the wavefunction, and no single measurement ever shows a smeared wave. Repeating the measurement many times reproduces the standing wave pattern in the statistics, so the two descriptions are not in conflict but are two aspects of one state, and the energy levels and the localised hits are both consequences of the same confinement.
